analysis: Examined the two changed files. (1) DaemonStateFile.swift: DaemonState.CoordinatorConnection (head lines 331-347) gains an optional lastRequestAt epoch-seconds field (nil before the first coordinator request), with a defaulted init parameter. It is diagnostic only, Optional, so older state files still decode, and the schema stays at 1. It adds only a timing/activity timestamp to a local file that already holds trust status, model lists and stats. DaemonStateFile.write (lines 641-652) is unchanged: it writes with default permissions via the atomic option, with no explicit owner-only mode. That is pre-existing, and the file is described as a read-only diagnostic. No new secret, key, prompt content or authorization material is persisted. The new field does not feed any authorization or serving decision in the supplied code. The state file is non-authoritative, and lifecycle commands use a separate mailbox (TB-003/TB-012). The activity timestamp is a minor local metadata exposure, below the bar for a finding. (2) DoctorRunner.swift: trafficDiagnostic adds a case .unconfirmed(detail) rendering an info-level diagnostic. It is display-only and does not grant or alter authorization. Because it is informational rather than a pass, it does not overclaim eligibility (T-052/T-056 are not weakened). The ServingReadiness.Verdict enum and its .unconfirmed producer (likely using lastRequestAt) are not in the supplied evidence. I could not verify that an unconfirmed verdict is never mapped to a more permissive state elsewhere, or that the exhaustive switch is satisfied in other callers. Integration should confirm in ServingReadiness that unconfirmed never upgrades authorization, and that the heartbeat or lastRequestAt recording introduces no coordinator-visible leak. No concrete security regression identified in the supplied units.
